    • Industry observers note that before you buy school supplies, gather last year’s leftovers, from backpacks and binders to calculators and pens, and cross everything that still works off the teacher’s list.
    • A leftover you reuse costs nothing this year, so it beats even back-to-school sale prices.
    • According to recent reports, families with kids in elementary through high school planned to spend an average of $146.45 on school supplies in 2026, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual back-to-school survey.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that before you buy school supplies, gather last year’s leftovers, from backpacks and binders to calculators and pens, and cross everything that still works off the teacher’s list. Then buy only what’s still missing, and get the basics during July’s back-to-school sales, when folders, notebooks, and crayons can cost under a dollar each.

    A leftover you reuse costs nothing this year, so it beats even back-to-school sale prices. And the priciest things a list asks for, like a backpack, a binder, or a calculator, usually outlast the school year.

    According to recent reports, families with kids in elementary through high school planned to spend an average of $146.45 on school supplies in 2026, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual back-to-school survey. Say two kids’ lists come to $120 at regular prices, and two backpacks and a calculator make up $60 of it. Reuse those three, buy the other $60 of supplies on July’s deals for about $40, and the year’s supplies cost $40 instead of $120. Three-quarters of that $80 saving comes from the backpacks and calculator you didn’t buy.

    In a recent development, start with the house. Empty last year’s backpacks, desk drawers, and pencil boxes, test every marker and glue stick, check zippers and straps, and write down what still works.

    In a recent development, then wait for the teacher’s list and buy only what it asks for, in plain versions rather than character-branded ones your child may outgrow by next year. If the list won’t arrive until the first week of school, buy pencils and notebooks in July and leave anything specific, like a binder size or a calculator model, until it does.

    Buy the basics in July, when office supply chains sell 2-pocket folders for 25 cents and boxes of crayons for 50 cents, often with a limit per customer. For a calculator or another item the list names by model, Staples and Office Depot will match another store’s lower price, though each excludes some sales. For supplies every child uses up, like pencils and glue sticks, a warehouse club’s bulk pack can cover all your kids. First compare its unit price, the price per item, with what each item costs on sale in July. Save the pricier items still on the list for your state’s sales tax holiday, if it has one.

    When school lets out, put whatever survived the year in one bin, and open it before you shop next summer.

    #148334. Latest Update: Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

    📅 16 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1499 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

    📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.
    • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
    • According to recent reports, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

    I thought to myself at the time,.

    “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

    According to recent reports, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

    I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

    In a recent development, among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

    According to recent reports, with all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

    Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

    When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

    While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

    Sources indicate that this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

    Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

    In a recent development, as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

    Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

    Recent findings suggest that in summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

    Industry observers note that my budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

    According to recent reports, this strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

    First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

    The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze proposal in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

    Industry observers note that but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

    Industry observers note that when it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

    I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,.

    Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

    For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

    Industry observers note that the only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I presently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

    Industry observers note that but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

    According to recent reports, in the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

    Sources indicate that but for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

    In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** Fresh points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

    In a recent development, this redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

    Industry observers note that midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

    Recent findings suggest that chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Flying Club are instant, making Chase the preferred transfer partner for time-sensitive bookings. Amex Membership Rewards also transfers 1:1 but may take 1-2 days.

    Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

    It has been revealed that virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

    Industry observers note that yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

    Recent findings suggest that the flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. You get dedicated check-in, priority boarding, the Heathrow Clubhouse lounge (which is excellent), a meal service, and a more relaxed travel experience. At 17,500 points, the per-point value (3-5 cents) makes it a strong redemption even for a short flight.

    Virgin Atlantic does add taxes and fees to award tickets, including some carrier-imposed surcharges. On short-haul European routes, total out-of-pocket costs typically run $50-$150 depending on the route and departure airport taxes. This is higher than some programs but still reasonable given the business class product.

    This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

    Sources indicate that the Virgin Atlantic short-haul European business class sweet spot is the perfect complement to a transatlantic award trip. At just 17,500 points, it costs less than most domestic economy awards while delivering business class service, Heathrow Clubhouse lounge access, and a stress-free connection to destinations across Europe. It is not the flashiest redemption in travel rewards, but it is one of the most practical: a building block that makes multi-city European itineraries accessible and affordable for the FI community.

    • According to recent reports, A money mistake you keep repeating starts with a thought that goes by fast, like “it’s all bad news anyway” when a bill arrives or “I deserve this” at the checkout.
    • Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, works on that thought, whether it leads to overspending, unopened bills, or a decision you keep putting off.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you keep making the same money mistake despite knowing better, work on the thought that sets the habit off. Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, teaches you to catch and test it, and a financial therapist pairs that work with money coaching. Start with a free self-help workbook, or ask your health initiative for a CBT therapist.

    According to recent reports, A money mistake you keep repeating starts with a thought that goes by fast, like “it’s all bad news anyway” when a bill arrives or “I deserve this” at the checkout. By the time you notice it, the envelope is in a drawer or the purchase is made.

    Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, works on that thought, whether it leads to overspending, unopened bills, or a decision you keep putting off. A therapist teaches you to spot it, test it against the facts, and practice a different response, with homework between sessions. The American Psychological Association reports that CBT has been shown to work for depression and anxiety disorders, and in many studies it has matched or beaten other talk therapies and psychiatric medication.

    Picture someone who leaves mail unopened for weeks and pays a late fee most months. Over eight sessions, he learns to catch the thought that it’s all bad news anyway, and he sets a 10-minute mail routine every Sunday. The late fees stop.

    Start on your own. The Centre for Clinical Interventions, a service of Western Australia’s Department of Health, offers free self-help workbooks, including one on procrastination that has you identify and test the excuses behind putting things off. For a habit with no worry behind it, like nightly takeout, swap in a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward.

    According to recent reports, A financial therapist combines work on your feelings about money with coaching on the money itself, so pick one when you want help with both. A financial planner works on goals such as retirement, and a credit counselor on your budget and debts.

    It has been revealed that financial therapy isn’t regulated in the U.S., so confirm that anyone you find in the Financial Therapy Association’s directory holds a mental health license or the association’s Certified Financial Therapist credential, CFT-I. For CBT, the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies lists licensed therapists you can search by zip code.

    Most individual and small-employer health looks must cover mental health care. Call the member services number on your insurance card and ask which therapists in your initiative’s network use CBT.

    Sources indicate that your first personal finance book should be the one written for the problem you have now, whether that’s getting started, paying off debt, investing, or how you think about money. Pick one, borrow it free from your library before you buy it, and put its one big idea to work before you open another.

    The best money books don’t promise a secret. Each one changes a habit, and these seven cover the habits most readers need, from a plan that fits on an index card to automatic saving, simple investing, and clearer thinking about money.

    So the right first book depends on where you are with money. An investing book won’t help much while you’re paying interest on a credit card balance, and a debt blueprint has little to teach someone who already pays their card balance in full every month.

    Here’s what each of the seven teaches, and the reader it suits.

    Name your problem, then start with its book: I Will Teach You to Be Rich for getting started, The Total Money Makeover for debt, The Index Card for investing, and The Psychology of Money for how you think about money. When you want more on investing than The Index Card’s rules give you, read one of the investing books for beginners built around index funds.

    According to recent reports, borrow your pick before you buy it, since your library card can get you the print copy free and often the ebook or audiobook too. Put its big idea to work before you start another book. Then save your money for the books you’d read twice.

    Look up your pick in Libby with your library card to borrow the ebook or audiobook.

    • It has been revealed that build a home gym from two or three pieces that fit the workouts you’ll actually do, not a full set.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that build a home gym from two or three pieces that fit the workouts you’ll actually do, not a full set. Resistance bands, a kettlebell, and a jump rope cover strength and cardio for about $75 new. Buy the kettlebell and other weights used, since iron doesn’t wear out.

    A corner of a room holds a working home gym, and each of the 12 pieces below costs less than $100 latest.

    Body-weight moves like squats, lunges, and pushups need no equipment, so buy a piece only when it adds something your body weight can’t, such as something to pull against, extra weight, or cardio that fits a small room.

    Recent findings suggest that match the pieces to the workouts you already do, or to the ones in your home workout plan. Bands and a kettlebell start a strength routine, a jump rope or a step covers cardio, and a mat and a foam roller cover yoga, Pilates, and stretching.

    In a recent development, say a beginner pays $45 a month for a gym she rarely uses. Bands, a 20-pound kettlebell, and a basic mat cost about $79 new, less than the $90 she pays for two months of dues. Canceling saves her $540 a year, so she’s $461 ahead after the first year, and all she gives up is machines and heavy weights she rarely used.

    Recent findings suggest that kettlebells and dumbbells are the pieces to buy used, since cast iron weighs the same after decades of use. Look for them on Facebook Marketplace, on Craigslist, and at used sporting goods stores such as Play It Again Sports, which buys and sells used fitness gear.

    The Play It Again Sports in Novi, Michigan, for one, charges 69 cents a pound for used dumbbells and 99 cents for new hex dumbbells, so a used pair of 10-pounders costs $13.80 there, $6 less than new.

    Buy bands newly introduced, since a set costs as little as $13 and rubber wears out. Performance Health, which sells TheraBand bands, states to check bands for tears, cracks, and other wear before each use and to replace any that show it.

    Most of the kit fits in a closet corner. Bands, a jump rope, sliders, and a suspension trainer share one bin, the mat and roller stand on end, and the weights sit on the floor beside them. A step with its removable feet taken off slides under a bed, which leaves the stability ball as the one piece that needs its own spot.

    Buy the two pieces your favorite workout needs, use them for a month, and add a third only when a workout you’ve kept up calls for it.

    #148321. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

    📅 25 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2592 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

    Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

    📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
    • Industry observers note that the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
    • This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

    Industry observers note that the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

    This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

    According to recent reports, is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

    As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

    Sources indicate that “The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

    Industry observers note that to answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

    A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

    When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

    According to recent reports, if the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

    Recent findings suggest that your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

    When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

    For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

    But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

    According to recent reports, now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

    But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

    In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

    So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

    Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

    But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

    Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a substantial Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

    This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

    Sources indicate that but what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more promptly?

    In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 big companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

    In a recent development, these are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

    If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

    What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

    What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

    Sources indicate that there’s one common theme in the major tech company boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

    Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

    It has been revealed that but that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

    According to recent reports, they may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

    The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

    According to recent reports, having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

    But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

    And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

    There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

    While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

    One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

    So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

    In a recent development, as I noted earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

    And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

    Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

    Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

    Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

    Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

    Sources indicate that for starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

    Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

    Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

    On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

    Recent findings suggest that just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

    Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

    Sources indicate that so far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

    Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

    It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

    What About Paying Off Your House?

    It has been revealed that over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

    Sources indicate that if you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

    Industry observers note that another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

    If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

    Recent findings suggest that then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

    In the Comments: what are your thoughts on the current stock market boom, future crashes and busts, and the role of Artificial Intelligence in our future?

    *although in my opinion it’s okay to check in weekly with The Economist, which has been my favorite source of world economic news for 32 years and counting.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can deduct only the medical and dental costs above 7.50% of your adjusted gross income, your income minus a few adjustments, and only if you itemize.
    • Recent findings suggest that for a retiree with $60,000 of adjusted gross income, which is her income after a few adjustments, the 7.50% threshold is $4,500.
    • It has been revealed that count what you paid out of pocket for doctors, hospitals, dentists, prescriptions, glasses, and hearing aids, plus the miles you drive to appointments at the IRS’s medical mileage rate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can deduct only the medical and dental costs above 7.50% of your adjusted gross income, your income minus a few adjustments, and only if you itemize. Count the health premiums you pay yourself, Medicare’s included. If you’re self-employed and can’t join an employer’s blueprint, deduct your premiums separately, with no threshold or itemizing, up to your business’s profit.

    Recent findings suggest that for a retiree with $60,000 of adjusted gross income, which is her income after a few adjustments, the 7.50% threshold is $4,500. With $9,000 of medical costs, Medicare premiums included, she can deduct the $4,500 above it if itemizing beats her standard deduction, which is bigger for anyone 65 or older.

    It has been revealed that count what you paid out of pocket for doctors, hospitals, dentists, prescriptions, glasses, and hearing aids, plus the miles you drive to appointments at the IRS’s medical mileage rate. Premiums count too, including Medicare Part B and Part D, coverage you buy yourself, and qualified long-term care insurance up to an IRS limit set by age.

    Nonprescription medicine other than insulin, most cosmetic surgery, and gym dues for general fitness don’t count. Neither do premiums your employer takes out of your pay before tax, or bills you pay from a health savings account, since that money was never taxed. IRS Publication 502 lists the rest.

    It has been revealed that if you’re self-employed, premiums for health coverage you buy on your own go on Schedule 1 instead, where they lower your adjusted gross income without a threshold or itemizing. Medicare premiums count there too, but the deduction can’t exceed your business’s profit. Any month you could join a subsidized initiative through your job or your spouse’s doesn’t qualify, and premiums the deduction doesn’t cover can count with your other medical costs.

    Industry observers note that costs count in the year you pay them, and a credit card charge counts in the year you make it, even if you pay off the card later. Say the retiree’s income stays at $60,000 and her costs run $6,000 a year. That clears her $4,500 threshold by $1,500 each year, or $3,000 over two years. The same $12,000 paid in one year clears it by $7,500, and that larger total is likelier to beat her standard deduction.

    Once this year’s costs get close to your threshold, have the dental work, hearing aids, or eye surgery you’ve been putting off done before December 31, and pay the bill by then.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

    Invoice Factoring – Worth the Fee Only When Waiting to Get Paid Costs More

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that invoice factoring turns your unpaid invoices into cash within days, but the factoring company keeps 1% to 5% of each invoice for every 30 days it goes unpaid.
    • A trucking, staffing, manufacturing, or wholesale business can finish a job and wait 30 to 90 days to get paid, while the bills for the next job come due now.
    • With factoring, you sell the unpaid invoice to a factoring manufacturer, or factor, which typically advances you 70% to 90% of its value within days.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that invoice factoring turns your unpaid invoices into cash within days, but the factoring company keeps 1% to 5% of each invoice for every 30 days it goes unpaid. Factor only when waiting would cost you more than that fee, and pick non-recourse factoring if one customer going broke would sink your business.

    A trucking, staffing, manufacturing, or wholesale business can finish a job and wait 30 to 90 days to get paid, while the bills for the next job come due now.

    With factoring, you sell the unpaid invoice to a factoring manufacturer, or factor, which typically advances you 70% to 90% of its value within days. The factor collects from your customer and sends you the rest, minus its fee. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce puts that fee at 1% to 5% of the invoice for every 30 days it stays unpaid.

    In a recent development, say a trucking tech giant factors $80,000 in invoices due in 45 days, with a 90% advance and a 3% fee. It gets $72,000 now and the last $8,000, minus the $2,400 fee, when its customers pay. That $2,400 is the same cost as borrowing the $72,000 for 45 days at roughly 27% a year.

    According to recent reports, the fee is worth paying only when the cash earns more than $2,400 in those 45 days, such as by funding loads the organization would otherwise turn down. If the $72,000 would sit in the bank until its customers pay, the $2,400 is wasted.

    A bank line of credit usually costs less than factoring, so get a quote on one first if your business qualifies. Factoring fits when you can’t get one or your sales have outgrown your credit limit, since the factor looks mostly at your customers’ credit.

    Recourse factoring costs less than non-recourse, but you repay the factor when a customer never pays. Non-recourse shifts that loss to the factor, so buy it if one big customer going broke would sink you. It usually covers only a customer that goes broke, not one that disputes the bill.

    In a recent development, before you sign, check the contract for a monthly minimum you must factor, a term of up to two years, and a fee to leave early. Then get the fees for invoices paid in 30, 60, and 90 days in writing, since a fee charged every 30 days triples when a customer takes 90 days to pay.

    #148312. Early-Payment Discounts Get You Paid Sooner – but 2/10 Net 30 Costs 37% a Year

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (512 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

    Early-Payment Discounts Get You Paid Sooner – but 2/10 Net 30 Costs 37% a Year

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An early-payment discount is an expensive way to get paid sooner.
    • On a $10,000 invoice, 2/10 net 30 means collecting $9,800 on day 10 instead of $10,000 on day 30.
    • Industry observers note that as an annual interest rate, that’s $200 ÷ $9,800 × 365 ÷ 20, or about 37%.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An early-payment discount is an expensive way to get paid sooner. Offering 2/10 net 30, 2% off for paying in 10 days instead of 30, costs you the equivalent of about 37% a year in interest. Offer one only when you need the cash and borrowing it would cost you more.

    On a $10,000 invoice, 2/10 net 30 means collecting $9,800 on day 10 instead of $10,000 on day 30. You give up $200 to get your money 20 days sooner.

    Industry observers note that as an annual interest rate, that’s $200 ÷ $9,800 × 365 ÷ 20, or about 37%. To check any other offer, divide what you give up by the cash you get early, then multiply by 365 divided by the number of days early.

    In the October survey by the National Federation of Independent Business, small business owners paid an average interest rate of 8.5% on loans of a year or less. At about 37%, 2/10 net 30 costs more than four times that 8.5%, so a line of credit near that rate is the cheaper way to cover a short cash gap. The same formula works on a factoring company’s offer to buy your unpaid invoices.

    Before you discount anything, send each invoice the day the work is done, which costs nothing. The discount is worth its price in a cash crunch, when a large unpaid invoice would leave you unable to make payroll and you can’t borrow the difference. With a customer who usually pays on day 50, the discount brings the money in 40 days early instead of 20, and its cost drops from about 37% a year to about 19%.

    Recent findings suggest that offer it only to the customers whose early payment you need. A printing company with no credit line, short of cash in its slow quarter, offers 1/10 net 30 to just its three largest accounts. They usually pay on day 30, so the printer collects $60,000 of invoices 20 days sooner for $600, about 18% a year, and everyone else still pays in full.

    According to recent reports, write the deadline as a date and both amounts in dollars. On a $5,000 invoice dated March 2, that’s “2% discount ($100) for payment received by March 12. Full $5,000 due April 1.” The word “received” means a check mailed on March 12 doesn’t count. Bill the $100 to any customer who takes the discount after March 12.

    For a line of credit to draw on instead of offering a discount, compare the best small business loans.
